sources.citation: Blackings, Mairi & Nigel Fabb. 2003. A Grammar of Ma'di. (Mouton Grammar Library 32.) Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter. [Google Books partial preview, id 2tANGFj-dUkC: pp. 1, 2, 7, 9, 40-42 saved as page images + search-within snippets]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: publisher record (DOI); no open copy and no library e-access found (also digitized at HathiTrust, search-only (in copyright); also a publisher record (DOI), probably paywalled)
sources.note: Describes LOKAI Ma'di [mhi], not snm. p. 42 sec. 3.5.5 'Absence of stress': 'We have not found evidence that, for any Ma'di word, a particular syllable predictably carries stronger stress than any other syllable. We therefore do not support Tucker and Bryan's (1966: 31) claim that stress is basically iambic (eg. final stress on a disyllable).' Three tones H/M/L (3.5); p. 40: loanword tone patterns may reflect source-word stress; 3.6.1 utterance-final emphasis by vowel lengthening. pp. 1-2: the Ma'di-Indri / 'Ma'di Okolo' of Rhino Camp, Arua District 'speak a language which more closely resemb…

sources.note: Second-hand only: 'Stress: Tucker and Bryan report that stress location varies among languages of the Moru-Ma'di group (which includes Logbara). Moru: stress on first syllable of disyllables. Ma'di: stress on final syllable.' Nothing Logbara-specific.

sources.harvard_location: Widener Library, call number 2235.4.26; Linguistics Library, call number CoPh 36.88
sources.note: Group-level survey statement: 'Even such intimately closely allied languages as MORU and MA'DI have quite different stress behaviour. In MORU stress is on the first syllable of disyllabic words.. In MA'DI, however, stress is on the final vowel: ˈléndrị, ˈléndr, iˈza, lɛ̀ˈdra. In both languages words within a phrase retain their original stress.' Nothing said about LUGBARA stress or about Okollo varieties. (Their MA'DI = Moyo/Sudan Ma'di [mhi].)

It is the only work that treats Okollo/Ogoko/Rigbo at all; p. 28 and p. 31 (sec. 3.1.6.5): 'The southern Ma'di dialects, spoken in the area of Rigbo, Ogoko, and Okollo, Uganda, should be considered Lugbara dialects, and more distant from Ma'di than other Lugbara dialects.'

Lugbara of Zaire 4 tones); no stress statement. fn. 3 clarifies that Andersen's 'S(outhern) Madi' means 'a variety of Madi spoken in Uganda' (Moyo Ma'di [mhi]), which is probably why Glottolog files his 1986 Afrika und Übersee Madi paper under sout2828.

sources.note: Ma'di LOKAI as spoken in Sudan [mhi]. Sec. 3 Tone (p. 130): 'There are three level tones; high, mid, and low. There are also downglides and upglides on phonetically long vowels.' Sec. 4 canonical patterns (open syllables, 1-4 syllables). No mention of stress anywhere.

sources.citation: Crazzolara, J. P. 1960. A Study of the Logbara (Ma'di) Language: Grammar and Vocabulary. London: Oxford University Press (for the International African Institute). [Rosetta Project scans: phonology chapter pp. 1-14, Introduction, Contents]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: HathiTrust digitized, search-only (in copyright); interlibrary loan (also digitized at HathiTrust, search-only (in copyright))
sources.note: Lugbara (Aivu/Arua dialect). Phonology + ch. 2 'Intonation' treat tone only (three level tones plus glides, verb tone rules); no statement on word stress ('Stressing of verbs' secs. 426-30 in the contents is grammatical emphasis). Intro sec. 7 p. viii: 'The most distant dialect is apparently that of the Ma'di-Ndri (also called Màdé) of the Olepi-Okolo area' -- i.e. Crazzolara counts the Okollo speech as a Logbara dialect but gives Ma'di-Ndri forms only exceptionally.
